top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: Endpoint-specific HRs were synthesized on the log-HR scale. For each HR, the standard error was calculated from the reported 95% CI as SE = [log(upper limit) - log(lower limit)] / 3.92. Separate random-effects meta-analyses were performed for OS and PFS/EFS using restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Pooled estimates were back-transformed and reported as HRs with 95% CIs. Between-study heterogeneity was summarized using I² and τ², and 95% prediction intervals were calculated to describe the expected range of effects in comparable future settings. PFS and EFS were grouped pragmatically because both capture progression- or event-related milestones prior to death; original endpoint labels were retained in study-level tables. 2.8 E-value analysis For protective associations, the inverse HR was used before applying the standard E-value formula. Confidence-limit E-values were calculated using the confidence bound closest to the null [16, 17]. ARTICLE IN PRESS E-values were interpreted as the minimum strength of association that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both receipt of hepatectomy and the survival outcome, conditional on measured covariates, to move the observed association to the null. This framework specifically addresses residual confounding rather than timing-related mechanisms.

top_evidence.text: The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261382843). This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement [11,14]. The literature search was updated during manuscript revision without changes to the prespecified PICO framework. No substantive amendments to the registered protocol were made. The complete database-specific search strategies are provided in Additional file 1 (Table S1).

top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: Regimen-based subgroup meta-analysis was not planned because treatment regimens were heterogeneous and sparsely represented within comparable hepatectomy contrasts. Prespecified descriptive diagnostics included leave-one-out analysis, exclusion of Kaplan-Meier-derived estimates, exclusion of extreme HRs, adjusted or time-dependent estimates only, directly reported HRs only where applicable, and influence diagnostics. Because the OS synthesis included 14 estimates, we assessed small-study effects and reporting-bias risk for OS using a contour-enhanced funnel plot, SE-based Egger regression, sample-size-based Peters-type regression, and rankcorrelation testing. The PFS/EFS synthesis included 10 estimates and combined related but nonidentical endpoints; therefore, its funnel plot and regression diagnostics were treated as descriptive only. These analyses were used to inform GRADE publication-bias judgments rather than to redefine the main synthesis. ARTICLE IN PRESS

top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: The 14 studies included analytic cohorts ranging from 36 to 1262 patients. Treatment contexts included tyrosine kinase inhibitor- and immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations, HAICbased strategies, TACE/HAIC-containing multimodal therapy, and real-world immune-based conversion regimens. Comparator definitions generally contrasted patients undergoing conversion or salvage hepatectomy with patients managed without hepatectomy after conversion-intent therapy. Time origin varied across studies. Some estimates were anchored at treatment initiation, some were conditional on response or conversion eligibility, and one study used a time-dependent Cox framework. Study characteristics are summarized in Table 1, with full study details in Additional file 1: Table S2. Endpoint-specific HRs with corresponding E-values are listed in Table 2, and the complete extraction table is provided in Additional file 1: Table S3. 3.3 Overall survival synthesis Fourteen OS-specific HRs were included. Conversion hepatectomy was associated with a lower hazard of death than non-surgical management (HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.22-0.48). Heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 65.7%; τ² = 0.307), and the 95% prediction interval included the null value (0.101.04) (Figure 2 and Table 3). 3.4 Progression/event-free survival synthesis ARTICLE IN PRESS Ten PFS/EFS-specific HRs were included. Conversion hepatectomy was associated with a lower hazard of progression or qualifying event than non-surgical management (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.280.59). Heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 64.3%; τ² = 0.197), and the 95% prediction interval included the null value (0.16-1.05) (Figure 3 and Table 3).

top_evidence.section: Results > Study Selection And Included Studies
top_evidence.text: Fourteen comparative survival studies met the eligibility criteria and contributed 24 endpointspecific HRs comparing hepatectomy with non-hepatectomy management, including 14 OS estimates and 10 PFS/EFS estimates (Figure 1).

top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: Eligible studies were full-text original clinical reports enrolling adults with initially unresectable, initially inoperable, or non-upfront-resectable hepatocellular carcinoma who received conversionintent treatment and were subsequently compared according to hepatectomy versus nonhepatectomy management. Eligible reports had to provide extractable comparative time-to-event HRs with 95% CIs for OS, PFS, EFS, DFS, or RFS, provided that the estimate explicitly isolated hepatectomy status. Reports were excluded if they were limited to initially resectable neoadjuvant populations, postoperative adjuvant-only treatment, transplantation-only downstaging, ablation-only conversion, non-original articles, case reports, duplicate cohorts, prognostic-factor-only analyses, or regimen-comparison analyses that did not isolate hepatectomy status. Locoregional, hepatic arterial infusion, systemic, and multimodal conversion-intent regimens were eligible when the report provided an extractable comparative HR for hepatectomy versus non-hepatectomy management. Initially unresectable disease was accepted according to the original study definition, protocol designation, or multidisciplinary treatment context [37]. We did not retrospectively impose a uniform technical unresectability definition across heterogeneous published cohorts. 2.3 Study selection and data extraction Study screening, data extraction, estimand classification, and risk-of-bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers using standardized, pilot-tested extraction forms to ensure consistency across the large volume of records. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or independent third-reviewer adjudication. For reports meeting eligibility criteria, we extracted study design, treatment context, analytic cohort size, comparison definition, survival endpoint, HR, 95% CI, time origin, exposure definition, HR source, adjustment method, adjustment status, covariates included in adjusted models when reported, and source location. ARTICLE IN PRESS For each extracted HR, we recorded whether the estimate was directly reported, modelderived, Kaplan-Meier-derived, adjusted, unadjusted, landmark-based, or time-dependent. HRs were not entered into synthesis unless the comparison isolated hepatectomy versus nonhepatectomy management. When the original report did not provide a single unambiguous time origin, the estimate was retained if the comparison was clinically interpretable, and time origin was coded as unclear for risk-of-bias interpretation and supplementary diagnostics. HRs for age, alpha-fetoprotein, portal vein tumor thrombus, tumor burden, radiologic response, pathological response, postoperative recurrence predictors, postoperative adjuvant therapy, and treatmentregimen comparisons were excluded unless hepatectomy status was explicitly isolated. An extraction table was maintained for all extracted comparative survival estimates (Additional file 1: Table S3).

top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: We assessed the certainty of the body of evidence for each synthesized outcome using an adapted GRADE framework. Certainty was judged separately for OS and PFS/EFS, considering study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias, and potential upgrading factors. ROBINS-I-informed domain judgments were used to inform the risk-of-bias domain, while heterogeneity statistics, prediction intervals, endpoint definitions, time-origin variability, and QBA findings informed the remaining domains. Because all included estimates came from non-randomized comparisons in which hepatectomy was usually assigned after treatment initiation, the GRADE assessment was specifically adapted to evaluate the certainty of these comparative prognostic and therapeutic associations.

top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: For OS (k = 14), the contour-enhanced funnel plot showed asymmetry, with several smaller estimates falling in statistically significant protective contours. SE-based Egger regression (t = - 3.71, p = 0.003) and rank-correlation testing (Kendall's tau = -0.47, p = 0.019) supported funnelplot asymmetry, whereas the sample-size-based Peters-type regression was not significant (t = 0.77, p = 0.456). This pattern suggests possible small-study effects, selective reporting, or true betweenstudy heterogeneity, but it does not prove publication bias. For PFS/EFS (k = 10), the funnel plot and regression diagnostics were treated as descriptive because the synthesis was at the minimum threshold and combined related but non-identical endpoints ( Figure S5 and Table S15).
